summaries.example: Imagine a family recipe passed from a grandparent to a parent and then to a child. Each person may change it, but the earlier people still affect what comes next. Yorck thought history works somewhat like this: people and generations pass along ideas, choices, feelings, and ways of living. New generations respond to what they receive.
summaries.summary: Paul Yorck von Wartenburg was a German philosopher who worked closely with Wilhelm Dilthey. Yorck argued that human beings are historical: we are formed by time, change, and links between generations. He called this historicity. He contrasted living history with the ontic, meaning things considered fixed, permanent, or simply present. Yorck thought philosophy had often focused too much on detached thinking and stable objects. He wanted it to notice the whole person, including feelings, choices, dependence on others, and personal responsibility. In his later unfinished writings, he described life as a changing balance among feeling, willing, and thinking. These parts of life can never settle into a final shape. Their movement helps produce history. Yorck also connected historical life with Christianity and a personal, transcendent God. His work became publicly known mainly after his death, especially through his published correspondence with Dilthey, and later influenced philosophers such as Heidegger and Gadamer.
key_ideas: People do not live outside history. Their lives grow through time and relationships with other generations.
Yorck distinguished changing, lived history from things treated as fixed and unchanging.
He thought feelings, choices, and thoughts all help shape human life.
History continues because people pass possibilities, ideas, actions, and conditions to those who come after them.
He believed philosophy should pay attention to the time and history in which people live.
Yorck gave special importance to personal feeling, responsibility, and a relationship with a God beyond the ordinary world.
summaries.why_it_matters: Yorck’s ideas encourage us to see people as more than separate minds studying a fixed world. Our memories, relationships, feelings, decisions, and inherited surroundings all help make us who we are. His view also asks philosophy to study its own time instead of pretending to stand outside history. This can help us ask better questions about how families, schools, communities, and generations shape one another.

important_terms.definition: The idea that human life is shaped by time, change, and connections with earlier and later generations.
A way of thinking about what is permanent or simply present, such as an object, number, or fixed idea.
Life as it is lived through change, memory, feeling, choices, and relationships across time.
A part or function of life involving feeling, choosing, or thinking about things.

questions_to_think_about: What parts of your life come from people who lived before you?
Can a person understand a choice without knowing anything about its time and place?
How might feelings change the way people understand history?
Is a fixed picture of the world always enough to explain a living person?

summaries.example: Suppose a society treats scientific explanation as the only serious way to understand human life. Yorck would ask what this approach leaves out: feeling, dependence, mortality, personal responsibility, and the historical conditions that made this intellectual style possible. He would not simply replace science with emotion. Rather, he would argue that cognition is one human function among others and that philosophy must examine how these functions are configured within a living historical world.
summaries.summary: Count Paul Yorck von Wartenburg was a German philosopher whose main philosophical partner was Wilhelm Dilthey. Their work helped establish historicity as a basic feature of human being. For Yorck, a human life does not merely exist as a present object. It develops through time, belongs to historical connections, and is shaped by predecessor and successor generations. This is why he distinguishes the historical from the ontic. The ontic concerns what is regarded as fixed, objective, or timeless; the historical concerns lived development and changing relations. Yorck’s central concern was ontology—the question of what kind of being human life is—rather than primarily the methodology of the historical sciences. He opposed metaphysical attempts to know reality from an eternal standpoint, arguing that philosophy itself is a historical expression of life and must interpret its own situation. His later fragments analyze primary life through three irreducible functions: feeling, willing, and cognition. Cognition and willing project outward, while feeling concentrates on inwardness. Their unequal and changing configurations create restless forms of consciousness, which become the motor of historical development. Yorck also gave a religious interpretation of this movement. He associated Christianity, especially Luther’s form of Christianity, with inwardness, freedom from worldly objectivity, personal responsibility, and relation to a transcendent God. The correspondence with Dilthey was published after Yorck’s death and helped bring his ideas to wider attention, including among later thinkers such as Heidegger and Gadamer.
key_ideas: Yorck and Dilthey developed historicity as a defining feature of human being, but Yorck focused more exclusively on the ontology of historical life than on the foundations of the historical sciences.
The ontic and the historical are fundamentally different: the former is treated as fixed or objective, while the latter is lived through time, change, and generational connection.
A person is a central historical category because individual agents transmit authority, sacrifice, ideas, powers, and material conditions to later generations.
Primary life is articulated through feeling, willing, and cognition. Their shifting balance produces unstable stances of consciousness and helps drive historical change.
Cognition projects objects into spatial distance and can abstract from temporality; feeling discloses inwardness and is tied to the experience of time, transience, and personal reality.
Yorck rejected knowledge from an eternal, history-free standpoint and argued that philosophy should become critical, historical, and practically attentive to human life.
summaries.why_it_matters: Yorck challenges the picture of philosophy as detached observation of timeless objects. His account links philosophical concepts to embodied, affective, willing, and historical life. It also offers a way to think about how generations are connected without treating history as a fixed script: people inherit conditions and possibilities, but they form new stances toward them. His emphasis on historicizing philosophy remains useful whenever a theory claims to explain human beings while ignoring its own historical standpoint.

important_terms.definition: The condition of human existence as intrinsically temporal, changing, and connected with historical development rather than merely present as a fixed thing.
What is treated as simply present, permanent, or objective, including physical entities, abstract objects, essences, and ideas.
The structure of connection through which persons and generations transmit ideas, powers, actions, and material conditions to successors.
A process by which life’s possibilities and effects are carried from individuals or generations into the lives of those who follow.
The lived structure of consciousness in which feeling, willing, and cognition are related but cannot be reduced to one another.
The outward projection involved in cognition and willing, contrasted with feeling’s more immediate awareness of inward life.
A stance in which life is oriented toward a God beyond ordinary worldly objectivity, rather than toward a metaphysical object within the world.
The philosophical demand that thinking recognize its own historical conditions and development.

questions_to_think_about: Does representing something objectively help us understand it, or can representation also distance us from its human significance?
Why might Yorck regard feeling and willing as necessary for judging what is real?
Can philosophy be both systematic and historical, rather than choosing only one approach?
How does Yorck’s account of generational transmission differ from the idea that each historical period is sealed off from the others?
What might be gained, and what might be risked, by connecting historicity with religious transcendence?

summaries.example: Think about how a school tradition changes over several years. Older students pass on rules, stories, and habits. New students inherit these things, but they may keep some, alter others, or reject them. Yorck would call this a historical connection between generations. The tradition is not just a frozen object; it is living because people feel, choose, and rethink it.
summaries.summary: Paul Yorck von Wartenburg was a German philosopher and a close collaborator of Wilhelm Dilthey. Yorck is especially known for the idea of historicity: human beings are formed by time, change, and historical relationships. A person is not merely an object that exists in the present. A person lives through development, memories, choices, feelings, and connections with other people and generations. Yorck called the fixed or timeless side of things the ontic. He thought the ontic and the historical should not be confused. A number, physical object, or abstract idea may be considered permanent, while human life is always moving and changing. Yorck understood history as a living connection. Earlier people pass on powers, ideas, influence, sacrifices, and material conditions. Later generations receive these inheritances and respond to them in their own way. In his unfinished philosophical fragments, Yorck described life through three basic functions: feeling, willing, and thinking. Thinking and willing reach outward toward objects and goals. Feeling is more closely connected with inward experience, including time, change, and personal attachment. None of these functions can be removed, and their shifting balance helps explain changes in historical life. Yorck wanted philosophy to become historical in its own practice. He rejected claims to knowledge from a completely eternal viewpoint and criticized forms of metaphysics that turn changing life into something fixed. He also gave his philosophy a religious direction, linking inwardness and personal responsibility with a transcendent God. His writings became influential after his death, especially when his correspondence with Dilthey was published in 1923.
key_ideas: Yorck believed human life is historical all the way through. We cannot fully understand people as if they were unchanging objects.
He and Dilthey emphasized historicity, but Yorck concentrated on what historical life is, while Dilthey also studied how the historical sciences can be justified.
Generations remain connected because they pass along ideas, actions, influence, and material circumstances.
Feeling, willing, and thinking are different parts of life. Their changing balance produces different kinds of people and historical periods.
Yorck criticized metaphysics when it tried to describe reality as if it could be known from a timeless viewpoint.
He connected inward feeling and personal responsibility with Christianity and with a God beyond ordinary worldly reality.
summaries.why_it_matters: Yorck helps explain why human beings cannot be understood in exactly the same way as objects in nature. People inherit a past, respond to it, and help shape what comes next. His ideas also show why philosophy may need both careful concepts and attention to lived experience. Asking how our own time influences our theories can make our thinking more self-aware and less likely to mistake one historical viewpoint for a timeless truth.

important_terms.definition: The idea that people are shaped by time, change, and relationships with earlier and later generations.
Something treated as fixed or simply present, such as an object, number, or unchanging idea.
The continuing flow of lived connections through which people and generations affect one another.
The passing on of effects, abilities, ideas, and conditions from earlier people to later ones.
The three basic ways Yorck says life is expressed: feeling, willing, and thinking or representing.
A way of understanding philosophy that notices its own time, history, and changing questions.
A reality beyond ordinary worldly objects and explanations; Yorck connected this idea with a personal God.

questions_to_think_about: How can a tradition stay connected to the past while changing in the present?
Why might Yorck think that studying only facts and objects misses part of human life?
Can feelings be a source of understanding, or do they only get in the way of clear thinking?
What does it mean for philosophy to study its own historical situation?
Why might a person’s choices matter to the history of later generations?
